e-8528.knowledge_point: Using a Percentage Points Table To Find the Z-Score for a Given Probability
e-8528.problem:
The table below gives the values of $\Phi^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p,$ where $p = \Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. Find the value of $z$ such that $P(Z \leq z) = 0.60.$

| $\quad p \quad$ | $0.60$ | $0.65$ | $0.70$ | $0.75$ | $0.80$ | $0.85$ | $0.90$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\Phi^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.2533\,$ | $\,0.3853\,$ | $\,0.5244\,$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ |
e-8528.worked_solution:
First, we express the given information in terms of $\Phi{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\le z) & =0.60 \\ Φ(z) & =0.60\end{aligned}
$$

So, we are looking for the value of $z$ such that

$$
z = \Phi^{-1} (0.60).
$$

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to $p = 0.60,$ and we find that

$$
p = 0.60 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \Phi^{-1}(p) = 0.2533.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z =  \Phi^{-1}(0.60) = 0.2533.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Using a Percentage Points Table To Find the Z-Score for a Given Probability
content.problem:
The table below gives the values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p,$ where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. Find the value of $z$ such that $P(Z\le z)=0.999.$

| $\,p\,$ | $0.900$ | $0.950$ | $0.975$ | $0.990$ | $0.995$ | $0.999$ | $0.9995$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.9600\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ | $\,2.5758\,$ | $\,3.0902\,$ | $\,3.2905\,$ |
content.worked_solution:
First, we express the given information in terms of $Φ:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\le z) & =0.999 \\ Φ(z) & =0.999\end{aligned}
$$

So, we are looking for the value of $z$ such that

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.999).
$$

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to $p=0.999,$ and we find that

$$
p=0.999\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(p)=3.0902.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.999)=3.0902.
$$
